cards.explanation: The answer is that Jacob asks Laban to send him on his way back home. Jacob, Isaac's son (Genesis 25:26), goes to Laban and says, “Send me on my way so I can return to my homeland.” He's asking to go home, not to set up shop where he is. The request is about leaving, and Laban is the one who has to answer it.

The answer is False. Jacob's family is part of the request. He says, “Give me my wives and children for whom I have served you, that I may go on my way.” He wants his wives and children given to him, not left with Laban. This family is not getting left at the rest stop, friends.

The missing word is blessed. Laban says, “I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you.” Divination is a way of seeking hidden answers, and Laban says that's how he learned it. Whatever his method, he names the LORD's blessing and ties it straight to Jacob. That's Laban admitting Jacob is good for business.

The answer is True. Jacob says it plain: “…you had very little before my arrival, but now your wealth has increased many times over.” That's Jacob making his case to Laban. He doesn't leave it at that, though, because he goes on to ask when he can provide for his own household. I'd call that a strong opening argument, friends.

The answer is the spotted and dark-colored animals. Jacob asks for “…every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat.” Then he says, “These will be my wages.” He's naming animals by their markings and color. That's his whole offer, and it comes with one condition.

The missing word is honesty. Jacob says, “…my honesty will testify for me when you come to check on my wages in the future.” He's inviting Laban to come look for himself. Then he spells out what would count against him: goats that are not speckled or spotted, or lambs that are not dark-colored, “…will be considered stolen.” That's a man leaving the cookie jar open and saying, “Count 'em.”
The answer is False. Laban takes the deal. He says, “Agreed,” and then, “Let it be as you have said.” No haggling, no counteroffer. I think that's a man who just wants to shake hands and move on.

The answer is Laban's own sons. Laban takes out the streaked or spotted male goats, the speckled or spotted female goats and every dark-colored lamb, and places them “…under the care of his sons.” Those are Laban's own sons. Notice it all happens “That very day…” and he doesn't wait around, bakers. I think a man that quick knows exactly what he's doing.

The answer is the white inner wood. Jacob takes fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees and peels the bark, “…exposing the white inner wood of the branches.” So what shows is white wood. A peeled branch looks very different from a bark-covered one, and that's what he sets out.

The missing words are watering troughs. Jacob sets the peeled branches “…in the watering troughs in front of the flocks coming in to drink.” The branches go right where the flocks come to drink. I think Jacob picked that spot with care. Location, location, location, friends.

The answer is True. The text says the flocks mated in front of the branches and “…bore young that were streaked or speckled or spotted.” That's what came out of it. Genesis tells us what happened and doesn't explain why. I think Jacob was watching those lambs and kids closely.

The answer is False, and Jacob is careful about it. The text says he “…set his own stock apart and did not put them with Laban’s animals.” Two flocks, two sets of animals, and he keeps a clear line between them. Honestly, I've never kept my sprinkles and my chocolate chips that organized.

The missing word is weak. The verse says, “…if the animals were weak, he did not set out the branches.” He only puts them out for the stronger females. The weaker ones don't get the branches. I think that's a man who knows exactly what he's doing.

The answer is False. The weaker ones go to Laban. The text says, “…the weaker animals went to Laban and the stronger ones to Jacob.” So Jacob ends up with the stronger animals. I think Laban got the short end of that stick, friends.

The answer is that he grows very rich. The text says, “Thus Jacob became exceedingly prosperous.” He owned large flocks, maidservants and menservants, and camels and donkeys. That's a long way from asking when he could provide for his own household. I think his accountant would've been smiling. And the story isn't over, bakers.
